title: Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts
content:
Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts
Songs that are largely or wholly created by AI have been banned from Australia's music charts.
From this week, all releases must be "substantially human made" to be eligible.
The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said the new code would help "promote the human nature of artistry".
It follows a controversy around a cover of Madonna's Like A Prayer by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz which recently topped the ARIA dance singles chart and peaked at number 2 on the country's overall chart.
The song has become a staple of commercial radio station playlists and been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify alone.
Fawaz later added generative AI credits to the song after a backlash.
ARIA said that Australian artists were competing for attention "in the most crowded market in history" and that it was "not interested in promoting or celebrating the success of AI-generated music that does not contain human artistry".
Under the new rules, AI assistance can still be used, but humans must have written the song, and have performed the lead vocal and primary instruments.
AI can also still be used for mastering songs and, for example, using drum machines and auto tune.
Earlier this year a song was banned from Sweden's music charts because it was created by AI.
And in July, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) said AI guidelines would be rolled out in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia for use in their official charts.
The updated code, based on the IFPI directive, also excludes music that raises "stream or chart manipulation concerns".
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said: "These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is, to say the least, a rapidly developing space."
"Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter."
She added: "A chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."
Artists will be required to declare AI use when they submit a song for chart consideration.
ARIA said that if it later emerged music was largely AI-generated it could retrospectively adjust chart positions, and if the piece topped the charts, it may request that awards given for reaching Number One were returned.
Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge their exclusion.
Among the artists supporting the move are Australian electronic act Peking Duk.
Last month, they shared an AI-assisted version of their 2014 hit High on Instagram, captioned: "When you re-record your own song with AI so Australian radio will play it."
Band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show that AI-generated music was "removing the human experience from life".
In July this year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese promised "the strongest possible protection" from AI for Australian creatives.
Albanese pledged that writers and musicians would be able to choose if and how their work was used in the training of AI, saying it would be "theft" if creatives lost that control and were not paid for its use.

report.summary: Australia's ARIA charts now ban largely AI-generated songs, requiring substantial human authorship, following a controversy over an AI Madonna cover.
report.background: The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) has updated its chart rules to require all releases to be 'substantially human made.' The decision follows an uproar over Australian DJ Josh Fawaz's AI-generated cover of Madonna's 'Like A Prayer,' which hit No. 2 on the national chart and amassed 48 million Spotify streams before he added AI credits after backlash. The new code aligns with broader global moves: Sweden banned AI-created songs earlier this year, and the IFPI is rolling out similar guidelines in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia. ARIA said the rules promote human artistry and also exclude music that raises stream manipulation concerns.
key_points: ARIA's new code requires songs to be substantially human made to qualify for Australian charts, meaning humans must write the song and perform lead vocals and primary instruments. AI assistance is still allowed for mastering, drum machines, and auto-tune, but the core creative work must be human.

The rule change was triggered by a viral AI cover of Madonna's 'Like A Prayer' by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz, which topped the dance singles chart and reached No. 2 overall. The song received heavy radio airplay and over 48 million Spotify streams, sparking backlash and debate over AI-generated music's place in official rankings.

Artists must declare AI use when submitting songs for chart consideration. If a song is later found to be largely AI-generated, ARIA can retrospectively adjust chart positions and may request that Number One awards be returned. Artists and representatives can challenge exclusions through an appeals process.

The move is part of a broader international push: Sweden banned AI-created music from its charts earlier this year, and the IFPI is implementing AI guidelines across several regions. ARIA's updated code is based on the IFPI directive and also aims to address chart and stream manipulation concerns.

Artists like Peking Duk publicly support the ban. The band shared an AI-assisted re-record of their own song to highlight how radio play can push artists toward AI, with member Adam Hyde saying AI-generated music removes human experience. The Australian government is also promising stronger protections for creatives over AI training use.
report.impact: For the AI music industry, the ban sets a clear precedent that wholesale AI-generated tracks cannot rely on official charts for legitimacy or promotion. It likely pushes developers toward building AI tools that augment human creativity—such as AI-assisted production, mixing, or arrangement—rather than fully autonomous song generators. For artists, the rules create a safer competitive environment and reinforce the value of human authorship, but also add compliance burdens. Regular listeners benefit from chart integrity, knowing that popular entries reflect human artistic effort. Globally, Australia's move could influence other markets to adopt similar standards, shaping how AI music is distributed, rewarded, and perceived.
report.tools: Musicians wanting to explore AI assistance while staying chart-eligible can experiment with open-source tools like MusicGen (Meta), Riffusion, and Hugging Face's AudioCraft, which generate instrumental ideas or textures but leave songwriting and performance to humans. Also keep an eye on IFPI and ARIA guidance updates, and AI-integrated DAWs like Ableton Live with AI plugins for mastering and sound design, which remain allowed under the new rules.
